analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal student aid and GI Bill money to college programs that don't prepare students for required licenses.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote in the House or Senate.
analysis.plain_summary: Many occupations — nursing, plumbing, cosmetology, and dozens more — require a state license before you can work. Some colleges, especially for-profit schools, enroll students in programs advertised as preparing them for those jobs, but the programs don't actually qualify graduates to sit for the licensing exam in their own state. The bill would make any such program ineligible for federal student aid, workforce grants, and military education benefits unless, within a year, it fully qualified students for licensure where they live and arranged the required clinical placements, internships, or apprenticeships. Schools would also have to certify their programs meet these tests, and could not relaunch a 'worthless' program under a new name after it lost funding.
analysis.who_benefits: Students who borrow federal loans, receive workforce grants, or use GI Bill and other military education benefits to pay for training in licensed occupations. Under the bill, their tuition dollars could only flow to programs that actually lead to a license in the state where they live or where the school advertised they could work — and schools would have to place them in required clinicals, internships, or apprenticeships on time. Veterans, who are heavily targeted by some for-profit recruiters, were explicitly covered through the military and veterans' benefits programs named in the bill.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and veterans using federal education aid

how_it_helps.text: Makes any program preparing students for a licensed occupation ineligible for federal aid unless it fully qualifies graduates to take the required exam and obtain the license in their own metropolitan area and state, and in any state the school advertised they could work in [S2] [S3].

Requires schools to arrange timely placement in pre-licensure requirements such as clinical placements, internships, or apprenticeships, which many students currently scramble to find on their own [S2] [S3].

Covers the full range of federal education money — Title IV student aid, workforce grants, adult education funds, GI Bill and other veterans' benefits, and military tuition programs — so schools could not switch a failing program from one funding stream to another [S3].

Requires the institution's most senior executive to personally certify that its gainful employment programs meet the new licensure-qualification tests, and bars resurrecting a program substantially similar to one that recently lost eligibility or was voluntarily discontinued for failing debt-to-earnings measures [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Schools whose licensed-occupation programs do not prepare students for licensure in the states where their students live — a category that includes many for-profit colleges — would lose access to federal student aid, GI Bill dollars, and workforce grants unless they restructured their programs within one year. Taxpayers and students who currently fund those programs would stop subsidizing credentials that do not lead to work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Schools whose programs don't lead to licenses

drawbacks.text: The one-year compliance deadline is short. Colleges would have to obtain programmatic accreditation, redesign curricula to match state licensing rules in every location they serve, and secure clinical placements quickly; a program that could not comply would lose federal funding rather than be phased out [S3].

Requiring programs to qualify students for licensure in the state where each student resides is difficult for online programs, which could be forced to restrict enrollment by geography or exit federal aid entirely, shrinking options for rural and working adult students [S3].
Cutting off federal aid is a blunt instrument: students already enrolled mid-program when a school loses eligibility could be left stranded without a way to finish their credential.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real but lopsided: the bill polices a specific, well-documented harm — borrowing federal money for a credential that cannot legally be used — while the main costs fall on the schools causing it. The legitimate concerns are the tight one-year timeline and the treatment of online and multi-state programs, which could push some borderline schools out of federal aid and strand current students. A more gradual phase-out would have addressed that, but the underlying consumer protection is straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees and two subcommittees for a year with no hearings, no markup, and no vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced the bill on December 14, 2017, with Rep. Mark Takano as its one cosponsor [S1] [S3] [S4].

The House referred it to three committees — Education and the Workforce, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs — a multi-committee referral that gives each committee separate veto power over the bill [S1] [S5].
It was then split among subcommittees: Veterans' Affairs' Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity and Armed Services' Subcommittee on Military Personnel, where it received no further action [S5].
No committee held a hearing or markup, the bill never reached the House floor, and it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Schools whose licensed-occupation programs fail to prepare students for the required licenses — often for-profit colleges — kept access to federal student aid, GI Bill dollars, and workforce grants without the new certification and placement requirements. Students and veterans kept bearing the risk of borrowing for credentials that don't qualify for licensure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Schools selling unlicensable credentials kept federal aid

for.name: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed it as consumer protection for students and veterans.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Armed Services and Veterans' Affairs Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill under the multi-committee referral and let it die in subcommittee without action.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats sponsored the bill and no votes or public opposition were recorded; it died in committee before any partisan position could form on the floor.

industries.note: These schools depend heavily on federal student aid, GI Bill dollars, and workforce grants, and some sell licensed-occupation programs whose graduates cannot sit for the licensing exam in their own state. The bill would cut off federal money to such programs, so its defeat preserved their revenue stream.

industries.industry: Nonprofit and community colleges with licensed-occupation programs
industries.note: The requirements apply to any institution taking federal aid, not just for-profits, so public and nonprofit schools with licensure-prep programs would face new accreditation, certification, and clinical-placement obligations — and risk losing aid if they cannot comply within a year.

The bill builds the accreditation system deeper into federal aid eligibility, requiring programmatic accreditation where licensing rules demand it and making accreditors the gatekeepers that determine whether a program keeps federal funding.
